blocks.text: Long before MCP existed, plenty of AI products already called external tools, a model would decide it needed to check the weather or search a database, and a developer had already wired up the code to make that happen. That older pattern still works fine today, and understanding exactly how it compares to MCP, what genuinely changes and what stays identical, makes it much easier to judge when MCP is worth reaching for and when it is not.
1. What "Traditional Tool Calling" Means Here

blocks.alt: A model calls a hand-rolled function
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875643-98120861.png

Traditional tool calling, in this lesson, refers to the pattern most AI products used before MCP, and many still use today: a developer writes a JSON schema describing a function, hands that schema to the model provider's API, and when the model decides to call it, the developer's own code intercepts that call and executes it directly, calling a database, hitting an internal API, running a script.

This is not a mistake or a legacy pattern to be ashamed of, it is simply a manual, hand-wired version of the same basic idea MCP eventually standardized, the model asks for something, code executes it, the result comes back. Every major model provider's API supports this today, often called function calling or tool use depending on the provider's own terminology.
1.1 Different Providers, Different Names

blocks.content: {"headers":["Provider","What they call it"],"rows":[["One major provider","Tool use"],["Another major provider","Function calling"],["A third provider","Function calling or plugins"]]}

blocks.text: The underlying idea across all of them is nearly identical, a schema goes in, a structured call to a named function comes out, only the field names and exact JSON shape differ from one provider to the next.
2. A Hand-Rolled Example, Start to Finish

Here is what a single tool integration typically looks like without MCP in the picture at all, a schema defined directly in the code that calls the model's API, and a matching block of logic that runs when the model asks to use it.

Every part of this, the schema, the dispatch logic, the actual fetch_forecast implementation, lives inside this one application's codebase. Nothing here is reusable by another team without copying and adapting the code by hand.
2.1 What Happens When You Add a Second Tool

Adding a second capability to the traditional example means adding a second schema entry to the same tools list and a second branch to the same if-else dispatch block, and a third, and a fourth. Nothing about this scales badly for a handful of tools, but the dispatch logic and the tools list grow together, tightly coupled, inside the one application that owns them.
3. What MCP Adds on Top of the Same Basic Idea

MCP does not replace the idea of a model deciding to call a function, that decision-making step is identical either way. What MCP adds is a standard, separate layer for defining and running that tool, one that is not glued directly into this one application's code, and not tied to this one model provider's specific schema format.

The get_forecast tool from the example above, rewritten as an MCP server, looks almost the same on the surface, but it now runs as its own independent program, reachable by any MCP-speaking host, not just the one application that happened to define it.

This layering is deliberate, MCP does not replace the model provider function calling format, it standardizes what happens on the other side of that call, once the model has decided what it wants to do.
4. Schema Definition: Bespoke Versus Standardized

blocks.alt: A bespoke schema is compared against an MCP standardized schema
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875644-909864870.png

In the traditional pattern, the tool schema is written directly against whichever model provider's expected format that specific integration targets, and providers do not all agree on the exact shape of that schema. Switching providers, or supporting two at once, usually means maintaining two slightly different schema definitions for the same underlying function.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Traditional tool calling","MCP"],"rows":[["Schema format","Whatever the model provider's API expects","One standard JSON Schema format, provider-agnostic"],["Where it lives","Inside the calling application's code","Inside an independent MCP server"],["Reused across providers","Only with manual adaptation","Yes, by design"]]}

blocks.text: 4.1 A Concrete Schema Mismatch Example

One provider might expect a top-level parameters field holding a JSON Schema object, while another expects an input_schema field with a slightly different required structure around it. A developer supporting both ends up maintaining two near-duplicate schema blocks describing the exact same get_forecast function.
5. Discovery: Hardcoded Lists Versus Live Discovery

blocks.alt: A hardcoded list is compared against live discovery
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875644-603659561.png

In the traditional pattern, the list of available tools is simply a Python or JavaScript list, written once by a developer and passed to the model on every request. If the underlying service adds a new capability, a developer has to notice, write a new schema entry, and redeploy the application before the model can use it.

MCP replaces that static list with the tools/list discovery call covered in MCP Workflow, run fresh at the start of a session. A server can add a brand new tool, and every connected client discovers it the very next time it asks, with zero code changes required on the client or host side.
5.1 The Cost of a Stale Hardcoded List

Imagine the weather service behind get_forecast adds a new optional units parameter, celsius or fahrenheit. In the traditional pattern, nothing about the model's available tools reflects that change until a developer edits the schema and ships a new release. In an MCP setup, the very next tools/list call simply returns the updated schema, no redeploy of the host required at all.
6. Portability Across Models and Vendors

blocks.alt: Traditional tool calling is tied to one model while MCP is portable
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875645-73486612.png

A traditional integration is written once, for one model provider's function-calling format. Adding support for a second provider commonly means writing a second, parallel set of schema definitions and dispatch code, even though the underlying logic being called is identical in both cases.

An MCP server, by contrast, does not target a specific model provider at all, it only speaks MCP. A host built around Model A can switch to Model B without touching a single MCP server, only the part of the host that talks to the model needs to change, exactly the vendor lock-in reduction discussed in the Why MCP lesson.
6.1 Switching Providers in Practice

A team migrating a traditional integration from one model provider to another typically has to rewrite every tool schema into the new provider's expected format and retest every dispatch path. A team using MCP servers migrates by changing only the part of the host that talks to the model, every MCP server keeps working completely unmodified through the switch.
7. Error Handling Conventions

Traditional integrations invent their own error handling convention, one team returns a plain string starting with "Error:", another raises an exception the calling code has to catch, a third returns a structured object with an ok field. None of these are wrong, but none of them are consistent from one integration to the next, either.

code.content:
# three different teams, three different conventions
return "Error: file not found"
raise FileNotFoundError(path)
return {"ok": False, "message": "file not found"}

blocks.text: MCP fixes this with one convention everywhere, a result with isError set to true, covered in detail in MCP Workflow, so any client, regardless of which server it is talking to, always knows exactly where to look for a failure.
A team that has already standardized on MCP error shapes gets this consistency for free across every server they connect to, rather than writing a separate error translator for each one.
7.1 Why Consistency Matters More at Scale

With one or two tools, inconsistent error handling is a minor annoyance a developer can just remember. With dozens of tools across several teams, inconsistent conventions become a real source of bugs, code written to catch one team's exception silently fails to notice another team's plain error string, and failures slip through unnoticed.
8. Security and Permission Boundaries

blocks.alt: Traditional tool calling has ad hoc security while MCP has a standard boundary
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875645-843747541.png

In a traditional integration, permission logic, which user can do what, which credentials get used, is usually scattered through the same application code that implements the tool itself, reinvented by whichever developer built that particular integration. In an MCP setup, that boundary sits at the server, a separate, independently auditable program whose access can be scoped and reviewed on its own, regardless of which host or model happens to be calling it.
8.1 Auditing an MCP Server Independently

Because an MCP server is a separate program with its own well-defined tool list, a security reviewer can examine exactly what it exposes and what credentials it holds without needing to read through the entire host application's codebase to find where a traditional integration's permission checks happen to live.
9. Maintenance Burden Over Time

blocks.alt: Traditional tool calling grows with each tool while MCP shares maintenance
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875950-228045582.png

A traditional integration's maintenance cost is paid entirely by the one team that built it, if the underlying service's API changes, that team fixes their one copy. An MCP server's maintenance is shared, if the community-maintained GitHub server gets updated for a GitHub API change, every team using that server benefits from a single fix, without any of them needing to touch their own code.
9.1 A Rough Numbers Comparison

blocks.text: 10. What Genuinely Stays the Same

It is worth being precise about what MCP does not change, because it is easy to overstate the difference. The model still decides, entirely on its own reasoning, whether and when to call a tool. The model still receives a schema and produces arguments matching it. The core request-then-execute-then-respond shape is identical in both worlds, MCP standardizes the plumbing around that shape, it does not replace the shape itself.

blocks.title: The one sentence version
blocks.content: MCP changes where a tool lives and how it is described and discovered, it does not change the fact that a model decides to call it.

blocks.text: 10.1 The Model's Own Perspective Barely Changes

From the model's point of view, both patterns look almost the same, a list of named functions with schemas, and the option to call one with matching arguments. The model is not aware of, and does not need to care, whether the code behind that function lives inline in an application or behind an MCP server on the other side of a client connection.
11. A Side-by-Side Comparison

blocks.text: 12. When Plain Function Calling Is Still the Right Choice

blocks.alt: A single app with a single tool makes plain function calling fine
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875951-887938387.png

MCP is not automatically the correct answer for every situation. A single internal script, used by exactly one small application, that will never be reused by anyone else and never needs to work with more than one model provider, gains little from the extra layer of a separate server process and a protocol handshake. Sometimes a five-line function passed directly to a model's API is simply the fastest, simplest, entirely appropriate solution.

items: A quick prototype or demo that will likely be thrown away.
A tool so tightly coupled to one specific application that no other host will ever plausibly need it.
A tiny hobby project where the overhead of running a separate server process outweighs any benefit.
A situation where you are locked into one model provider anyway and portability genuinely does not matter.

blocks.text: A tiny prototype with exactly one tool and no plans to reuse it elsewhere is a perfectly reasonable place to skip MCP entirely, the standardization only pays off once reuse or scale enters the picture.
12.1 A Quick Decision Checklist

items: Will more than one application ever need this exact tool? If yes, lean MCP.
Will this need to work across more than one model provider? If yes, lean MCP.
Is this a throwaway prototype with a short lifespan? If yes, plain function calling is fine.
Does the tool need almost no isolation or review, and change constantly alongside the one app that uses it? If yes, plain function calling is simpler.

blocks.text: 13. A Worked Example: Same Feature, Two Approaches

Consider a feature that looks up a customer's order status. Built the traditional way, a developer writes a schema and a dispatch function directly inside the one customer-support chatbot that needs it, done in an afternoon, working only for that one bot.

Built as an MCP server instead, the same lookup logic gets wrapped as a get_order_status tool exposed by an independent orders server. The customer-support chatbot uses it exactly the same way, but so can an internal Slack bot, a mobile app's assistant, or next year's replacement chatbot, all without rewriting the lookup logic even once.
14. Common Mistakes When Comparing the Two

items: Assuming MCP changes how the model decides to call a tool, it does not, that reasoning step is identical either way.
Wrapping every tiny internal script in an MCP server out of habit, even when nothing will ever reuse it.
Underestimating how much a hardcoded tool list costs to maintain once a service changes shape a few times a year.
Believing traditional tool calling is now obsolete, plenty of legitimate, well-run products still use it and always will.
Forgetting that switching to MCP does not remove the need to review what a tool is allowed to do, it just relocates that review to the server.

blocks.text: 15. Practice: Decide for Your Own Tool

Think of one tool your own project, or a hypothetical one, might need, a lookup, an action, a search. Write down honestly whether it will ever be used by more than one application or need to work with more than one model provider.

code.content:
my_tool = "..."
reused_by_other_apps = True  # or False
supports_multiple_model_providers_needed = True  # or False
# if both are False, plain function calling may genuinely be the simpler choice

blocks.text: If either answer is genuinely yes, sketch what that tool would look like as an MCP server instead, and compare how much extra work that actually represents versus the traditional approach.
Key Takeaway

Traditional, hand-rolled tool calling and MCP share the exact same core idea, a model decides to call something and gets a result back, MCP simply standardizes where that something lives, how it is described, and how it is discovered, trading a little extra setup for portability and reuse across teams and models.

This lesson compared MCP against a hand-wired, code-level alternative, the next lesson, MCP vs APIs, compares it against something different again, calling a traditional REST API directly, and why MCP behaves more like a thin, standardized layer on top of an API than a replacement for one.
